> *On a random split, registry fields explained about a quarter of the
> variation in trial duration. Tested on later trials, they explained
> almost none—and that finding became the point.*

::: callout-warning
## Correction (October 2026)

Earlier versions of this post reported a random-split R² of **0.84** and
a time-based R² of **0.04**, and attributed the gap to temporal drift.
Both figures were wrong. A date-parsing bug (`lubridate::ymd()` read
month-only registry dates such as "2005-08" as 2020-05-08) mis-dated 609
trials, dropped 975 others, and produced the spurious 0.84. A follow-up
check also found 74 Phase 2/3 trials counted twice. The data have been
rebuilt and the models retrained; the numbers below are the corrected
ones. The conclusion—registry data cannot forecast trial
duration—still holds. The size of the random-split result does not.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [1. Framing the problem]{.smallcaps}

Forecasting clinical trial timelines is an appealing problem in
pharmaceutical analytics. Timelines influence portfolio planning,
resourcing, and cross-functional expectations across R&D organizations.
At the same time, experienced trial teams recognize that duration is
shaped by factors that are difficult to observe early—protocol
complexity, enrollment dynamics, site performance, and evolving
standards of care.

This project approaches trial duration forecasting as a **validation
problem first**, rather than an optimization exercise. The objective is
not to produce an operational forecasting tool, but to evaluate what
level of prospective signal is realistically supported by publicly
available registry data.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [2. What question this analysis tests]{.smallcaps}

The core question is intentionally narrow:

**Can ClinicalTrials.gov registry features support prospective
forecasting of oncology trial duration?**

To answer this, I built an end-to-end modeling pipeline and Shiny
dashboard using completed oncology treatment trials. The target variable
is registry-defined duration (Start Date → Completion Date), which may
include extended follow-up and should not be interpreted as a direct
proxy for last-patient–last-visit (LPLV); predictors are limited to
registry fields (phase, sponsor type, enrollment, sites, countries, and
registration-to-start lag). Several of these are final reported values
rather than what was known at study start, which, if anything, flatters
the model. A check confirms how much: refitting with only what is known
at study start (phase, sponsor, registration-to-start lag) drops R²
from 0.24 to 0.10 on a random split and from 0.03 to −0.07 on later
trials, worse than predicting the average. Most of the signal comes
from inputs known only in hindsight.

The emphasis is on aligning validation strategy with intended use,
rather than maximizing retrospective fit.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [3. When random validation appears convincing]{.smallcaps}

Using a conventional random train/test split, the model appeared to
perform well:

-   R² ≈ 0.24 (mean of five random splits)\
-   Median absolute error ≈ 21 months

That is modest, but it suggests registry fields carry some signal.
However, random splits mix trials from the same years into training and
test sets, so era-specific patterns are shared between them. The split
measures how well the model describes history, not how well it forecasts
new trials. For a forward-looking use case, this validation strategy is
inappropriate.

At this stage, the model was answering the wrong question.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [4. What changes under time-based validation]{.smallcaps}

When the validation strategy was changed to reflect prospective
use—training on trials started by 2015 (n = 2,079) and testing on trials
started 2016–2018 (n = 378)—almost all of that signal disappeared. The
trials, features, recipe and tuning grid are the same in every row; only
the split, or the test trials it is scored on, changes:

| Validation Approach                      | Test R²  | Median Absolute Error |
|------------------------------------------|----------|-----------------------|
| Random split                             | 0.24     | 21 months             |
| Random split, test trials ≤ 112 months   | 0.13     | 18 months             |
| **Time-based split**                     | **0.03** | **15 months**         |

R² here is 1 − SSE/SST on log duration. The middle row scores the random
split only on trials that fit the same window as the time-based test set
(explained below). The squared correlation between predicted and actual
is 0.24, 0.16 and 0.11 for the three rows.

Three things explain the result:

1.  **Registry feature limitations**: Key drivers of duration—protocol
    complexity, endpoint strategy, enrollment velocity, and operational
    execution—are largely absent from ClinicalTrials.gov. What signal
    the registry fields do carry is weak and partly specific to the era
    the model was trained on.
2.  **Right-truncation of the test window**: Only completed trials are
    included, so a trial started in 2016–2018 had to finish by the
    January 2026 data pull (the longest ran 112 months), while earlier
    trials could run up to 15 years. Long trials are missing, so the
    test set runs shorter (on average about 13% shorter than predicted)
    and slightly narrower than the training data, and both lower R². Scoring the
    random split on the same window cuts its R² from 0.24 to 0.13:
    roughly half of the gap (40–80% across five splits, and probably
    more, since the check uses one 112-month cap) is the window, and
    the rest is the cost of predicting later trials.
3.  **Later trials look shorter, partly by construction**: median
    duration is 64 months for trials started by 2015 and 52 months for
    2016–2018, but among the earlier trials no longer than 112 months
    the median is 56. Most of the apparent shortening is the truncation
    above, not a change in practice. It also explains a puzzle in the
    table: errors in months get *smaller* as R² falls, because the
    missing long trials are the ones a model misses by the most months.
    Neither metric is immune to the window; the middle row is the
    fairer comparison.

Under these conditions, low prospective R² is not a modeling failure.
The time-based number is, if anything, a pessimistic estimate because
of the truncated window, but even the most generous comparison leaves
registry fields explaining a small fraction of the variation.

The result is also robust to how the cohort was defined. The oncology
cohort comes from a keyword-based registry query, and about 8% of
modeled trials (203 of 2,457) list no cancer term in their conditions
field. Refitting without them moves test R² from 0.030 to 0.018 and
leaves the conclusions unchanged.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [5. Why this matters in pharma analytics]{.smallcaps}

In pharmaceutical decision-making, forecasts are used prospectively: to
inform planning, resource allocation, and expectations. Validation
strategies that mix past and future data can materially overstate
confidence and lead to incorrect conclusions.

This case study demonstrates that **how a model is validated matters
more than which algorithm is chosen**. All four algorithms tried were
statistically tied in cross-validation. A model that describes history
modestly but fails under time-based testing may still be useful
diagnostically—but it should not be positioned as a forecasting tool.

From an analytics governance perspective, this distinction is critical.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [6. What this project does—and does not—claim]{.smallcaps}

This project demonstrates:

-   How to design validation strategies that align with prospective use
-   How the choice of split changes the answer, and why right-truncation
    must be accounted for when comparing eras
-   How registry-only features constrain forecasting power

It explicitly does **not** claim:

-   That oncology trial duration is predictable from registry data alone
-   That this model should be used for operational timeline planning
-   That algorithmic complexity would resolve the observed limitations

The results are conditional on the data sources and features used.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [7. What would be required for planning-grade forecasting]{.smallcaps}

If the objective were operational forecasting, additional data would be
required, including:

-   Protocol complexity and amendment history
-   Endpoint structure and follow-up requirements
-   Enrollment trajectory and screen-failure dynamics
-   Site and geography-level performance history
-   Competitive and standard-of-care context

These factors are typically available only through internal systems, not
public registries.

## [Dashboard Preview]{.smallcaps}

> The dashboard is structured to make validation behavior visible and to
> discourage overinterpretation of point predictions.

**Executive Brief** Surfaces key metrics (R², MAE, sample size) with
appropriate caveats about prospective use limitations.
![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poncest/clinical-trial-forecaster/main/screenshots/executive_brief.png)

**Duration Forecaster** Interactive scenario sandbox for exploring how
trial characteristics relate to predicted duration—positioned as
educational, not operational. Each estimate comes with the range that
2016–2018 test trials actually landed in relative to their estimates
(pooled across all test trials, with the upper end likely too low),
which makes the model's uncertainty visible.
![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poncest/clinical-trial-forecaster/main/screenshots/forecaster.png)

**Feature Explorer** Visualizes Elastic Net coefficients and feature
distributions to understand which registry variables the model weighted.
![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poncest/clinical-trial-forecaster/main/screenshots/explorer.png)

**Model Performance** Diagnostic plots comparing actual vs. predicted
duration, with error breakdown by phase and sponsor type.
![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poncest/clinical-trial-forecaster/main/screenshots/performance.png)

**Methods & Data** Documents the data pipeline, inclusion criteria, and validation methodology—including the key lesson on why time-based validation matters.
![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poncest/clinical-trial-forecaster/main/screenshots/methods.png)

## [Appendix: Methodology & Build Notes]{.smallcaps}

### [Analytical Pipeline]{.smallcaps}

1.  **Data acquisition** – ClinicalTrials.gov API (oncology
    interventional trials)
2.  **Cohort filtering** – Treatment purpose, Phase 1/2 through Phase 3,
    completed studies
3.  **Feature engineering** – Log transforms, ratios, categorical
    encoding
4.  **Validation design** – Time-based split aligned to prospective use
5.  **Modeling** – Elastic Net regression via tidymodels
6.  **Diagnostics** – Error analysis and residual inspection

### [Model specification]{.smallcaps}

-   **Algorithm:** Elastic Net (glmnet)
-   **Target:** Log-transformed duration (months)
-   **Cross-validation:** 10-fold CV within training data only
-   **Baseline comparisons:** Linear regression, Random Forest, XGBoost
-   **Selection criterion:** One-standard-error rule on cross-validated
    RMSE; all four models were within one standard error of the best,
    and Elastic Net was kept by a stated preference for a regularized
    linear model (at the small penalty chosen, it is nearly identical
    to linear regression). The 2016–2018 test set was not used for
    model selection
-   **Random vs time-based comparison:** Same cohort, recipe and grid;
    five random splits, each also scored on a truncation-matched subset,
    vs the time-based split
-   **Robustness check:** Refit excluding trials with no oncology term
    in their conditions field (test R² 0.030 → 0.018)

### [Technical stack]{.smallcaps}

-   **Language:** R
-   **Framework:** Shiny (modular architecture)
-   **UI:** shiny.semantic (Appsilon)
-   **Modeling:** tidymodels
-   **Visualization:** ggplot2, ggiraph, reactable
-   **Deployment:** shinyapps.io

### [References]{.smallcaps}

-   ClinicalTrials.gov – U.S. National Library of Medicine
-   Tidymodels documentation – https://www.tidymodels.org/
-   Appsilon shiny.semantic – https://appsilon.github.io/shiny.semantic/
-   Wong, C.H., Siah, K.W., & Lo, A.W. (2019). Estimation of clinical
    trial success rates and related parameters. *Biostatistics*, 20(2),
    273–286.

## [Closing reflection]{.smallcaps}

::: callout-note
The most important outcome of this project is not a performance metric,
but a methodological lesson: **honest validation protects
decision-makers from false confidence**.

In trial analytics, recognizing the limits of available data is as
important as extracting signal from it.
:::
